newsitem.title: USA: Gourmet fruitcake alive and well, despite the jokes.
newsitem.headline: Gourmet fruitcake alive and well, despite the jokes.

text.p: Despite jokes to the contrary, the millions of pounds of fruitcake served each year from Thanksgiving to New Year's will not end up as part of a massive stockpile of inedible confections.
Fruitcake will actually get eaten.
Bakers of gourmet fruitcake, filled with nuts, fresh pineapple, fancy cherries, whole eggs and butter, say appetites for their products have not dulled in the least.

"How long does your fruitcake last? Until you get the top off the tin," joked John Crawford, a partner in the 100-year-old Collin Street Bakery in Corsicana, Texas, which will turn out about 4 million pounds of fruitcake this season.

Collin Street, the world's largest gourmet fruitcake baker, claims to have a million customers in its database, ranging from companies that buy thousands of cakes to give as gifts to two "spinster ladies" who buy one each year and split it, Crawford added. Celebrity customers include game show hostess Vanna White and Monaco's Princess Caroline.
Out of deference to the teetotalers of the world, Collin Street does not put any alcohol in its cakes, but does include instructions on how to "doctor" them with brandy or bourbon.

West Point Market, a food and wine speciality shop in Akron, Ohio, expects to sell 30 cases of fruitcake. Each case contains 12 pounds of either one-, two- or three-pound fruitcakes, priced between $10.99 for a one-pound cake to $29.99 for three pounds.
"(Customers) buy it for themselves as well as for gifts," said Russell Vernon, owner of West Point Market.
So what about the joke that there are really only a few hundred fruitcakes in existence that keep getting passed -- untouched and uneaten -- from person to person over the years?
Gourmet fruitcake elitists blame run-of-the-mill, sticky, two-dollar cakes full of orange and lemon peel.
"I had been exposed to the old dry ones with the green and red things in it, turnip, orange peel and things like that," said Ronald Young, sales manager for Grandma's Bake Shoppe in Beatrice, Neb.

Then Young went to work for Grandma's, the second largest gourmet fruitcake baker in the world, and he became a true believer. "People who say they don't like fruitcake, if they try a sample of ours, we have a convert," Young said.
Grandma's fruitcake includes a mixture of rum, bourbon and brandy, although the alcohol evaporates in the baking.
Trina Creighton, an anchor/reporter for KMTV Channel 3 in Omaha, Neb., got a sample of Grandma's evangelism when she made an on-air joke about fruitcake.
Creighton joked during a segment on cleaning out the refrigerator that no one knows how long fruitcake is good for since nobody eats it. In rebuttal, Grandma's sent a fruitcake.
"The newsroom inhaled it," Creighton said.
But it is easy to see a fruitcake could inspire a bit of humour.

For example, Harry and David, the mail order food and fruit retailer, converted an industrial cement mixer to make its fruitcake confection, a sweet, fruit-and-nut laden dessert. But that was only so it can tumble the fruit and nuts together while keeping them whole, explained Diana McLaughlin, public relations coordinator.

Harry and David each year sells "tens of thousands" of the fruit cake confection, a product it introduced in 1947, McLaughlin said. It sells an equal amount of a more traditional fruitcake each year, which has a more cakelike texture.

Crawford said Collin Street's specially packaged fruitcakes are perfect for shipping because of the longevity of the product. "We ship (fruitcakes) into Bangladesh. It takes 90 days to get there by surface mail," he said. "And they arrive on time."

But not every fruitcake is meant to be eaten. Callaghan Promotions of Birmingham, Mich., is offering for a fourth year a recyclable fruitcake that comes with a shipping label so it can be passed on to someone else.

The fruitcakes, which are available for $8.95 only through Metro Gift, a Royal Oak, Mich., mail order company, are marked with the last few years and the next five or six, said Kevin Callaghan, who came up with the idea.
"So you can check off the year that you get it and pass it on," Callaghan said.
